title: Conditionals I: たら (と as the contrast)

grammarPoints.rule: たら is the cheapest thing in this whole level. Take the plain past — the た-form you have made since module 11 — and put ら on the end. たべた becomes たべたら, いった becomes いったら, ふった becomes ふったら. That is the entire construction: no new conjugation, nothing to memorise beyond "the past form, plus ら". It means "if/when X happens", and what follows is what happens next. The verb at the END of the sentence carries the tense, exactly as it did for まえに — たら itself never says when.

examples.en: If it rains, I'll stay home.

antiPattern.ja: あめが ふるたら、いえに いる。
antiPattern.why: ら goes on the PAST form, never the dictionary form — ふる becomes ふった first: あめが ふったら、いえに いる。

grammarPoints.rule: English makes you choose. "If it rains" doubts the rain; "when it rains" expects it. Japanese does not make you choose, and たら is the same word for both. 「あめが ふったら」 is if-or-when, and the sentence never says which — the listener works it out from whether the thing is likely. That is not Japanese being vague. It is Japanese leaving out a distinction English is forced to carry, the same way it leaves out the difference between one book and some books. Do not go looking for a second form for "when"; たら is it.

examples.ja: はるに なったら、はなが さく。
examples.en: When spring comes, the flowers bloom.

examples.ja: あした あめが ふったら、いかない。

grammarPoints.rule: Here is what たら can do that と cannot, and it is the practical half of this module. The second clause of a たら sentence may be anything at all — a request, an invitation, a want, a plan. 「えきに ついたら、でんわを して ください」. 「やすみに なったら、うみに いきたい」. Nothing is blocked, because たら only claims that one thing follows another and makes no claim that it always does. Whenever you are unsure which conditional to reach for, たら is the safe answer.

examples.ja: えきに ついたら、でんわを して ください。
examples.en: When you get to the station, please call.

examples.ja: やすみに なったら、うみに いきたい。
examples.en: When the holidays come, I want to go to the sea.

examples.ja: うちに かえったら、しゅくだいを して ください。
examples.en: When you get home, please do your homework.

grammarPoints.rule: と is the other conditional, and it says something stronger: EVERY TIME. Put the dictionary form in front of it and と claims the result is automatic — this is how the world works, not what you expect on this one occasion. Seasons are the clearest case: 「はるに なると、はなが さく」, and nobody has to decide whether the flowers feel like it. Anything mechanical behaves the same way, which is why you will meet と all through the sentences below on switches and engines. The form could not be simpler, because nothing changes at all: dictionary form, then と. What you are choosing when you reach for it is not a tense — it is a claim about the world.

examples.en: When spring comes, the flowers bloom.

antiPattern.ja: はるに なったと、はなが さく。
antiPattern.why: と takes the DICTIONARY form, never the past — たら is the one that takes た: はるに なると、はなが さく。

grammarPoints.rule: Directions are the everyday place と lives, and for the same reason as the seasons: a road does not sometimes lead to the station. 「この みちを まっすぐ いくと、えきが ある」 — go straight and the station is there, every time, for everyone. This is why you will hear と constantly the moment you ask somebody the way, and why the answer almost never comes back with たら: the person giving directions is describing the town, not guessing about you.

grammarPoints.rule: と has ONE restriction and it is the whole contrast lesson. Because と claims the result is automatic, the second half cannot be something you are asking for, suggesting, ordering or planning — those are all things that might not happen, and と has already promised that this one always does. ×「えきに つくと、でんわを して ください」 is broken as a shape. Swap in たら and it is fixed: 「えきに ついたら、でんわを して ください」. So the test is mechanical rather than a feel: look at the END of the sentence. If it is ください, ましょう, たい, つもり, or a plain command, you need たら.

examples.ja: えきに ついたら、でんわを して ください。
examples.en: When you get to the station, please call.

examples.ja: この ボタンを おすと、ドアが うごく。

examples.en: When winter comes, it snows.

antiPattern.ja: えきに つくと、でんわを して ください。
antiPattern.why: と promises the result always happens, so its second half cannot be a request — たら takes those: えきに ついたら、でんわを して ください。

grammarPoints.rule: One ready-made phrase, and it is the politest way to suggest something in the language. Hang どうですか on a たら clause and you have "how about ~ing?": 「いしゃに いったら どうですか」. It is softer than a suggestion because it never actually says what you should do; it asks the other person what they make of the idea. 〜たら いい is the same shape making a recommendation instead of a question — 「はやく ねたら いい」, you'd do well to sleep early. Both are just たら with something on the end, so there is nothing new to build.

examples.ja: いしゃに いったら どうですか。
examples.en: How about going to a doctor?

examples.ja: ちかてつに のったら どうですか。

examples.ja: せんせいに きいたら どうですか。

examples.ja: ちかみちを とおったら いい。
examples.en: You'd do well to take the shortcut.

grammarPoints.rule: Two suffixes that make a number approximate, and the only thing to get right is which one takes which kind of number. ごろ goes on a POINT in time — 「さんじごろ」, around three o'clock. ぐらい goes on an AMOUNT — 「じゅっぷんぐらい」, about ten minutes; 「せんえんぐらい」, about a thousand yen. A clock time takes ごろ, a quantity takes ぐらい, and the tell is whether you could ask "how long" or "how many" about it. ごろ also replaces に when it lands on a time — 「さんじごろ いく」, not 「さんじごろに いく」.

examples.ja: さんじごろ うちに かえる。
examples.en: I'll go home around three.

examples.ja: えきまで じゅっぷんぐらい かかる。
examples.en: It takes about ten minutes to the station.

examples.ja: この ほんは せんえんぐらいだ。
examples.en: This book is about a thousand yen.

examples.ja: しちじごろ ごはんを たべる。
examples.en: I eat around seven.

examples.ja: ちかてつに じゅっぷんぐらい のったら、うみに つく。
examples.en: If you ride the underground for about ten minutes, you reach the sea.

antiPattern.ja: さんじぐらい うちに かえる。
antiPattern.why: a point on the clock takes ごろ, not ぐらい — ぐらい is for amounts: さんじごろ うちに かえる。

lessons.title: 「ボタンを おすと」 — the result that never varies
lessons.focus: と's claim is stronger than たら's: not what happens this time, but what happens every time

beats.stem: その ボタンを おすと きかいが とまるから、しごとが
beats.en: If you press that button the machine stops, so when work finishes please press it
beats.explanation: the first half is a fact about the machine and takes と; the second half is a request and takes たら. One sentence, both forms, and the endings decide which goes where.

beats.audio: しごとが おわったら、ちかてつに のって うみに いきたい。
beats.answer: When work finishes, I want to take the underground and go to the sea
distractors: When work finishes, I want to take the bus and go to the sea
If you take the underground to the sea, work finishes
When work finished, I took the underground to the sea

beats.audio: うちから えきまで じゅっぷんぐらい かかる。
beats.answer: It takes about ten minutes from home to the station
distractors: It takes about ten hours from home to the station
I'll leave home for the station around twenty past
It takes about ten minutes from the station to home

lines.speaker: Tanaka
lines.ja: やすみに なったら、なにを しますか。
lines.en: What'll you do when the holidays come?

lines.speaker: Mika
lines.ja: うみに いきたいです。ちかてつに のると、じゅっぷんぐらいです。
lines.en: I want to go to the sea. It's about ten minutes on the underground.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.ja: あめが ふったら？
lines.en: And if it rains?

lines.speaker: Mika
lines.ja: うちで ほんを よむ。はやく おわったら、でんわを して ください。
lines.en: I'll read at home. If you finish early, please call.

questions.q: Which of Mika's sentences could NOT have used と?
options: 「はやく おわったら、でんわを して ください」 — it ends in a request
「ちかてつに のると、じゅっぷんぐらいです」 — it names a time
Both of them could use と
Neither of them could use と
questions.answer: 「はやく おわったら、でんわを して ください」 — it ends in a request

beats.ja: やすみに なったら うみに いきたいけど、あめが ふったら いかない つもりだ。
beats.en: When the holidays come I want to go to the sea, but if it rains I don't intend to go
